lesson.title: Measuring Current: Why the Meter Has to Get In Line
lesson.summary: Measuring current requires breaking the circuit open and inserting the meter in series, so that all of the current is forced to flow through it, the opposite connection style from voltage measurement, and mixing the two up is a common and damaging mistake.
lesson.body:
Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a circuit, so to measure it, the meter has to actually be in that flow, not just touching in from the side. This means measuring current requires a fundamentally different connection than measuring voltage: you must open the circuit at the point where you want to know the current, and insert the meter's leads into that gap so that every electron passing through that part of the circuit has no choice but to pass through the meter first. This is called a series connection, and it is the defining requirement of current measurement.

Here is the mistake this catches out even experienced hobbyists: after getting comfortable touching a voltmeter across two points without breaking anything, it is tempting to do the same thing with the meter set to measure current, simply landing both probes across a component while it is still fully wired into the circuit. This is a serious error. An ammeter is built with a very low internal resistance, because it needs to add almost nothing to the circuit it is measuring, so connecting it in parallel across a component effectively places a near short circuit right next to that component. The meter suddenly tries to carry far more current than it was ever designed for, which typically blows the meter's internal fuse instantly and, in circuits with enough available current, can damage the meter or the circuit before the fuse even has a chance to act.

The correct procedure is to identify the point in the circuit where you want to know the current, disconnect one lead of a component or wire at that point to create a deliberate gap, and connect the meter's probes across that gap so the meter becomes part of the current path itself. Many multimeters also require you to move the red probe to a separate jack, often labeled mA or A, specifically for current measurement, precisely because that input is wired straight through the meter's low resistance shunt rather than through the high resistance path used for voltage. Getting the jack wrong is a second, related mistake worth watching for on any given meter: check the panel before you connect.
